James Baldwin. The writer and social critic whose essays, novels, and plays explored identity, race, sexuality, and morality with unflinching moral clarity. His work became a cornerstone of the Civil Rights era, blending autobiographical depth with prophetic urgency about American racial violence and hypocrisy.

Baldwin emigrated to France in 1948 as a young writer seeking refuge from American racial prejudice, though he remained engaged with the American civil rights struggle. He wrote Go Tell It on the Mountain in 1953, an autobiographical novel drawing on his childhood in Harlem and his initial religious convictions. Then came Giovanni's Room in 1956, a groundbreaking novel about homosexual desire that treated gay experience with existential seriousness rather than pathology.

The essay collection Notes of a Native Son, published in 1955, became canonical for its meditations on race, identity, and American society. It established his voice as a moral authority on these questions. His speech A Talk to Teachers, delivered in 1963, and essays like The Fire Next Time articulated the psychological cost of racism on both Black and white Americans. He also adapted his play Blues for Mister Charlie in 1964 from a real murder case, turning it into an indictment of American racial violence. Like Richard Wright before him and Ralph Ellison alongside him, Baldwin grappled with systemic racism and the question of how to maintain artistic integrity under oppression.
